   Bad weather is believed to have contributed to the crash of a business jet in Florida that killed nine people. In Europe, hoax bomb threats prompted multiple flight diversions and emergency landings. 

   Delta CEO Ed Bastian took to LinkedIn to blast London Heathrow Airport’s decision to relocate his airline’s operations to a different terminal from its partners at Virgin Atlantic. Meanwhile, American Airlines is the first major U.S. carrier to resume nonstop flights to Haiti in years.

   And the U.S. Coast Guard detained a cruise ship in Miami, prompting operator MSC Cruises to cancel a sailing after travelers had already boarded. 

       Globe-trotting amid gridlock?     TOM BRENNER/GETTY IMAGES   As I watched the midterm results roll in this week, I couldn’t help but wonder what it meant for travelers. After all, in the past year alone we’ve seen multiple government shutdowns that created major headaches for fliers—even though Republicans controlled Congress and the White House. 

   I posed the question to Geoff Freeman, CEO of the U.S. Travel Association, a lobbying group that represents the travel industry. His takeaway: “I think we’re about to enter the two craziest years we’ve ever seen.”

   Here are five things travelers should watch out for following the midterm elections:

   1. Will there be more shutdowns? 

   If the Democratic-controlled Congress and the Trump White House don’t see eye-to-eye on upcoming budget bills, chaos could come to our airports . Lawmakers have yet to pass legislation that would ensure TSA workers are paid in any future shutdowns. (The TSA has begun researching vendors who could offer paycheck advances in these instances, according to a notice .)

   2. Will the Iran War end? 

   Vice President JD Vance blamed the Middle East conflict for the GOP’s fate this election. If that were to lead to a quicker resolution to the war, flying through Middle Eastern hubs such as Dubai and Doha could become easier. Whether fuel prices—and airfares—will fall as a result isn’t clear.

   3. Will international visitors return? 

   There’s been a “Trump Slump” in foreign visitors to the U.S. since President Trump’s second term began. Even during the World Cup this summer, the number of people visiting the U.S. from abroad was down. Travel executives attribute this both to rhetoric coming out of the White House, as well as policies that tourists find discomforting such as social-media screenings at border checkpoints.

   If international visitation remains depressed, domestic tourists could benefit if that leads to deals for destinations like Las Vegas or Orlando.

   4. Will the dollar weaken? 

   Following Tuesday’s election, the dollar dropped to a one-month low compared with a basket of other currencies. If political gridlock causes the dollar to lose more strength, taking trips abroad could become more expensive for Americans. (Fewer jaunts to Paris for shopping sprees , in other words.) 

   5. Will Congress take on credit-card companies? 

   The two sponsors of a bill that would regulate fees tied to credit cards are both leaving Congress: Democratic Sen. Dick Durbin of Illinois is retiring, and Republican Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas lost his re-election bid. Trump supports the proposal, and other lawmakers may fill the void. But you probably don’t need to worry about your credit-card rewards anytime soon.

What Travelers Need to Watch Out for After the Midterms
 
Plus, one airline is hiking bag fees, and hoax bomb threats are causing chaos in Europe’s airspace
 

Happy Friday! This is WSJ travel reporter Jacob Passy filling in for Dawn Gilbertson, who is off on a much-deserved vacation. Here’s what you might have missed if you were glued to midterm-related news this week:

 

Bad weather is believed to have contributed to the crash of a business jet in Florida that killed nine people. In Europe, hoax bomb threats prompted multiple flight diversions and emergency landings.

 

Delta CEO Ed Bastian took to LinkedIn to blast London Heathrow Airport’s decision to relocate his airline’s operations to a different terminal from its partners at Virgin Atlantic. Meanwhile, American Airlines is the first major U.S. carrier to resume nonstop flights to Haiti in years.

 

Beginning today, Southwest passengers in most fare classes will be able to make same-day flight changes or add their names to standby lists on the airline’s app (or on the website 24 hours before departure).

 

Brace for higher checked-bag fees. JetBlue quietly hiked prices for checking luggage this weekend—its second increase this year. When it did this back in March, other carriers soon followed.

 

And the U.S. Coast Guard detained a cruise ship in Miami, prompting operator MSC Cruises to cancel a sailing after travelers had already boarded.

 
 
 

Globe-trotting amid gridlock?

 
 
TOM BRENNER/GETTY IMAGES
 

As I watched the midterm results roll in this week, I couldn’t help but wonder what it meant for travelers. After all, in the past year alone we’ve seen multiple government shutdowns that created major headaches for fliers—even though Republicans controlled Congress and the White House. 

 

I posed the question to Geoff Freeman, CEO of the U.S. Travel Association, a lobbying group that represents the travel industry. His takeaway: “I think we’re about to enter the two craziest years we’ve ever seen.”

 

Here are five things travelers should watch out for following the midterm elections:

 

1. Will there be more shutdowns?

 

If the Democratic-controlled Congress and the Trump White House don’t see eye-to-eye on upcoming budget bills, chaos could come to our airports. Lawmakers have yet to pass legislation that would ensure TSA workers are paid in any future shutdowns. (The TSA has begun researching vendors who could offer paycheck advances in these instances, according to a notice.)

 

2. Will the Iran War end?

 

Vice President JD Vance blamed the Middle East conflict for the GOP’s fate this election. If that were to lead to a quicker resolution to the war, flying through Middle Eastern hubs such as Dubai and Doha could become easier. Whether fuel prices—and airfares—will fall as a result isn’t clear.

 

3. Will international visitors return?

 

There’s been a “Trump Slump” in foreign visitors to the U.S. since President Trump’s second term began. Even during the World Cup this summer, the number of people visiting the U.S. from abroad was down. Travel executives attribute this both to rhetoric coming out of the White House, as well as policies that tourists find discomforting such as social-media screenings at border checkpoints.

 

If international visitation remains depressed, domestic tourists could benefit if that leads to deals for destinations like Las Vegas or Orlando.

 

4. Will the dollar weaken?

 

Following Tuesday’s election, the dollar dropped to a one-month low compared with a basket of other currencies. If political gridlock causes the dollar to lose more strength, taking trips abroad could become more expensive for Americans. (Fewer jaunts to Paris for shopping sprees, in other words.) 

 

5. Will Congress take on credit-card companies?

 

The two sponsors of a bill that would regulate fees tied to credit cards are both leaving Congress: Democratic Sen. Dick Durbin of Illinois is retiring, and Republican Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas lost his re-election bid. Trump supports the proposal, and other lawmakers may fill the void. But you probably don’t need to worry about your credit-card rewards anytime soon.
